title: Create an account and sign in
summary: How to create an account on Blipmade, confirm the address and open the first session.

blocks.text: An account holds your services, your domains, your invoices and your support tickets. The registration asks for your first name, your last name, the address of your email and a password.

items.title: Fill in the registration form
items.body: Open the page Create account and fill in the fields First name, Last name, Email address and Password.
items.result: The form refuses an address that another account already uses and a password that does not meet the rules.

items.title: Confirm the address
items.body: Open the message that the platform sent to the address of the account and follow the link of the message.
items.result: The address is confirmed and the page offers the button Go to your dashboard.

items.title: Sign in
items.body: Open the sign-in page, write your address and your password and sign in.
items.result: The dashboard of your account opens.

blocks.text: The platform answers the same way for every address, on the sign-in page and on the page of the forgotten password, so it never tells you whether an account exists.
The password is checked before it is accepted, and the form writes down what is missing.

rows.v: At least 10 characters, and at most 200.
At least one lowercase letter and one uppercase letter.

blocks.text: A password manager is the easiest way to hold a long password that follows the rules.
There is no API of keys today. A program that talks to the platform uses the session of an account.

sections.title: Sign in, sign out and the sessions

blocks.text: A session lasts fourteen days and is not extended by the activity. When it ends, the page asks you to sign in again. You can see the open sessions of the account and close them at any time from the settings.

items.q: I forgot the password.
items.a: Open the sign-in page, follow the link called 'Forgot password?' and use the link of the message that arrives. Choosing a new password ends every session of the account, including the one on your phone.

items.q: The page says that the email address or the password is not correct.
items.a: The address and the password are checked together, so the message does not tell you which of the two is wrong. Check the address and try again, or follow the link called 'Forgot password?' under the password field.

items.q: I do not receive the message with the confirmation link.
items.a: Look in the folder of the junk mail and in the folder of the spam. If the message does not arrive, ask for a new link on the sign-in page or open a support ticket.

blocks.text: The dashboard of the account shows the services you have, the catalog of the products and the state of your invoices. The first step is to order an application.

Read [Deploy your first app](/docs?p=first-app) next. [The dashboard of your account](/docs?p=dashboard) tells you where everything is, and [Your profile, your address and your sessions](/docs?p=account) tells you what you can change about the account.

title: Deploy your first app
summary: How to order an application, what the platform writes into the container and how to open the service.

blocks.text: The catalog holds the apps and the databases that can be ordered. Every entry carries its own resources and its own price.

items.title: Pick the product
items.body: Open Deploy in the menu and pick the product in the catalog. The card of the product shows the memory, the vCPU and the storage it needs.
items.result: The page of the product opens with the resources and the price of the entry.

items.title: Choose the resources
items.body: Give the instance a name, choose the memory, the vCPU and the storage, and choose the options you want. The estimate follows every change.
items.result: The button Review order is available.

items.title: Review the order
items.body: Check the configuration and the price of the order and choose Continue to payment.
items.result: The page of the payment opens.

items.title: Place the order
items.body: Choose Pay and deploy.
items.result: The platform starts the deployment and the page shows the steps of it.

items.title: Open the instance
items.body: When the deployment is finished, choose Open instance.
items.result: The page of the instance opens with the tabs of the service.

blocks.text: The platform cannot take a payment today, so the checkout is refused and the order stays unpaid. The deploy page says it in these words: Checkout is not available. The order was created and stays unpaid. Open a support ticket to finish the payment.

sections.title: What the deployment writes into the container

blocks.text: A deployment writes a minimal Node.js application into the container and starts it with npm run start. The container runs the Node.js image of the platform.

The application answers on the health path of the product with a small JSON document that carries the name of the product, the state and the time the container has been running. Every other path answers with a line of text that names the product.

The product itself is not installed by the platform. The name in the catalog is the name of the product, and what runs in the container is the application of the platform until you put your own files there.

items.title: Open the address of the instance
items.body: The address of the instance is on the page of the instance. Open it in a browser.
items.result: The application answers with the code 200.

items.title: Read the output of the container
items.body: Open the tab Console of the instance. The output of the container is written there, and the field Command lets you send a command to the service.
items.result: You see the line that says the application listens on the port of the allocation.

blocks.text: The platform writes three files into the container: package.json, index.js and README.md. The README.md of the container says that the code of the product replaces them.

sections.title: If the service does not answer

items.q: The address does not answer at all.
items.a: Check that the instance is started: the tab Overview shows the state and the buttons Start, Restart and Stop. Then open the tab Console and read the output of the container.

items.q: The deployment failed.
items.a: A deployment that could not be delivered is refunded by the platform, and the event is written in the events of the instance. See [Refunds and credits](/docs?p=refunds).

items.q: My application answers on another port.
items.a: The container has to listen on the port of its allocation; the port of the allocation is given to the container in SERVER_PORT. An application that listens on another port is served to nobody.

items: Put your own code in the container: [the files of the instance](/docs?p=files).
Give the service an address of your own: [Domains and SSL](/docs?p=domains).
Keep a copy of the files: [Backups](/docs?p=backups).
Change the size of the service when it needs more: [Choose the right resources](/docs?p=resources).

title: Your profile, your address and your sessions
summary: What the settings of the account hold and how to change the name, the address, the password and the sessions.

blocks.text: The settings of the account hold the name, the address and the password. Everything else of the account has a page of its own: the services, the domains, the invoices and the tickets.

rows.v: The first part of the name. The platform writes it in the messages it sends you.
The second part of the name of the account.
The address where the platform writes to you. A new address is only used after the link of the confirmation.
The role of the account on the platform. The account you create yourself is a customer account.

blocks.text: The address of the account is also where the platform writes about your services: a deployment that is finished, an invoice, a change of resources that was refused.

sections.title: Change the address of the account

items.title: Open the settings
items.body: Choose Settings in the menu and open the panel Profile.
items.result: The fields of the account appear.

items.title: Write the new address
items.body: Fill in the field New email address and send the form.
items.result: The platform writes a confirmation link to the new address. The account keeps the old address until the link is used.

items.title: Confirm the new address
items.body: Open the message that arrives at the new address and follow the link of the message.
items.result: The new address is the address of the account.

blocks.text: An address that another account already uses is refused. Only one request is open at a time: a new request replaces the one that is waiting for its confirmation.

items.title: Open the settings
items.body: Choose Settings in the menu and open the panel Password.
items.result: The fields Current password, New password and Repeat the new password appear.

items.title: Write the new password
items.body: Fill in the three fields and save the form.
items.result: The password of the account is changed.

blocks.text: The sessions of the other devices end with the change. The session you are using stays, so you are not signed out of the page you are on.
The rules of the password are the same as when the account was created: at least ten characters, a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter and a number.
The panel Sessions lists the sessions that are open for the account, with the device and the date of each one. The session you are in is marked with This device.
A session lasts fourteen days and is not extended by the activity. You can end one session, or all the other sessions at once.
A session you do not know is a reason to change the password. The change ends the other sessions of the account.
The panel Account of the settings closes the account. The platform asks for your password and for the words CLOSE MY ACCOUNT, so a request is never made by mistake.
The request is recorded. Your services keep running until the end of the period you paid for, and the team writes to you before anything is closed. A request can be taken back while it is open.
Closing the account is not the same as cancelling an instance. The data of a cancelled instance is kept for the term of retention: see [Cancel an instance](/docs?p=cancel).

title: The dashboard of your account
summary: What the pages of the dashboard show and where the actions of the platform are.

blocks.text: The menu of the dashboard holds the same eight entries on every screen:

items: Overview — the state of the account: the services, what needs your attention and the last events.
Deploy — the catalog of the apps and the databases that can be ordered.
Apps & databases — the services you have, with the state of each one.
Domains — the hostnames of your services and their certificates.
Email — the mailboxes of the platform and the hosted mail.
Billing — the estimate of the month, the subscriptions and the invoices.
Support — the tickets you opened and the answers of the team.
Settings — the profile, the address, the password, the sessions and the notifications.

blocks.text: The Overview page is the first screen after the sign-in. It carries a tile for the number of your services (Services), the total of the month (Monthly total), the services that need you (Needs attention) and the way into the catalog (Deploy).

items: Deploy your first app — the panel that is there when you have no service yet.
Needs attention — the services that need you: a service whose status is failed, degraded or suspended, and a service whose subscription payment is past due.
Your services — the list of your instances, with the state of each one.
Recent activity — the last event of every service.

blocks.text: Every service opens on a page of its own. The tabs are the same for every product:

items: Overview — the state, the address and the actions of the service.
Console — the output of the container and the field to send a command.
Files — the file browser of the container.
Databases — the databases that belong to the instance.
Backups — the copies of the files that you made.
Network — the address and the port of the service.
Startup — the image, the command and the environment of the container.
Schedules — the tasks that run in the container.
Settings — the name of the instance and the cancellation.
Activity — the events of the instance.
Resources — the memory, the vCPU and the storage of the instance.
Domains — the hostnames that point at the instance.

items.title: Deploy an application
items.body: Open Deploy and pick a product in the catalog.
items.result: The configuration of the instance opens.

items.title: Put your own code in the container
items.body: Open the tab Files of the instance and upload your own files over the files that the platform wrote.
items.result: The service that starts is yours.

items.title: Give the service an address
items.body: Add a hostname of your own in the tab Domains, or use the address of the allocation.
items.result: The service answers on the name you chose.

title: WordPress
summary: What a deployment of WordPress writes into the container today, and what the platform does not install.

blocks.text: WordPress is the most widely used content management system. It is a PHP application that needs a web server, a PHP runtime and a database of its own.
A deployment of WordPress writes a minimal Node.js application into the container and starts it with npm run start. The container runs the Node.js image of the platform.

The WordPress application itself is not installed by the platform today: {{planned}} a WordPress installation with its own PHP, its own web server and its own database. The name in the catalog is the name of the product, and what runs in the container is the application of the platform until you put your own files there.

The product page of the catalog shows the entry: the category, the minimum of resources and the price. The deploy page carries the state of the entry: an entry that cannot be ordered says so there and the order is blocked.

rows.v: A Node.js application in a container, started with npm run start

items.title: Open the address of the instance
items.body: The address of the instance is on the page of the instance. Open it in a browser.
items.result: The application answers with the code 200.

items.title: Read the answer of the health path
items.body: The health path of the product answers with a JSON document that carries the name of the product, the state and the time the container has been running.
items.result: You see the name of the product and the time it has been running.

blocks.text: The platform writes three files into the container: package.json, index.js and README.md. The README.md of the container says that the code of the product replaces them.
The platform sets no environment variable that you have to fill in. The tab Startup of the instance shows it in these words: No variables. The container starts without any environment variable.

A WordPress that you install yourself asks for the connection details of its database and for its own salts. The platform sets none of them: write them in the tab Startup of the instance, with Add a variable.

sections.title: Put your own code in the container

items.title: Open the tab Files
items.body: The file browser of the instance shows the files of the container. The files that the platform wrote are package.json, index.js and README.md.
items.result: The tree of the container is there.

items.title: Upload your own files
items.body: Use the action that uploads a file to the instance and write your files over the files of the platform. A text file can also be changed in place with Save file.
items.result: Your files are in the container.

items.title: Check the start
items.body: The tab Startup shows the command the container runs when it starts: npm run start. The start script of your package.json has to run your code.
items.result: The command is the one your package needs.

items.title: Restart the instance
items.body: Use the button Restart on the tab Overview.
items.result: The console shows the output of your application.

blocks.text: A file that you have changed is left exactly as it is: the platform only repairs the files that are still its own.

sections.title: Read the output of the service

blocks.text: The tab Console of the instance shows the output of the container as it is written, and the field Command lets you send a command to the service. The state of the console is written at the top of the panel: Connected, Connecting or Disconnected.
The platform does not keep a history of the output. If your application has to keep a log of its own, write it to a file of the container and read it in the tab Files.
The backups are made by you, on demand, from the tab Backups of the instance. The platform copies the files of the container into an archive that you can download and restore.
Nothing makes a backup on a schedule and the platform keeps no history of them. Take a backup before you change something big in the container.
A backup is a copy of the files of the container. It is not the export of the instance, which describes the service and its records: see [Cancel an instance](/docs?p=cancel).

sections.title: Change the size of the service

blocks.text: The tab Resources of the instance shows the memory, the vCPU and the storage that the service has, and the price of the month.
A change of resources is an order that has to be paid, and the service is restarted when the change is applied. Read [Upgrade or resize an instance](/docs?p=upgrade) before you change anything.

sections.title: When the service does not answer

items.q: The container answers, but I expected WordPress.
items.a: The deployment writes the application of the platform, not WordPress. Put the files of your WordPress installation in the container yourself, and check that the container runs the image and the command that your installation needs.

items.q: The address answers with a line of text instead of my site.
items.a: That line is the answer of the application of the platform. It stays as long as the files of the platform are the ones that run.

items.q: My WordPress installation does not start.
items.a: The container runs Node.js. A WordPress installation needs PHP and a web server, and the platform does not provide them in the container today. Read the output of the container in the tab Console to see what the start command says.

items.body: Open the instance and choose the tab Databases.
items.result: The tab Databases shows the databases that belong to the instance.

items.title: Create the database
items.body: Fill in the fields Name of the database, User of the database and Password, and leave the allowed address as it is if the connection comes from the instance itself.

items.body: Choose Credentials to see the host, the port, the user and the password of the database.

items.a: The catalog of the platform does not offer Redis today, so there is nothing to order. When the catalog carries the product, the page of the product opens and the order can be placed.

items.a: A database of an instance is kept on the node of the instance, and the allowed address of the database decides who may open a connection to it. Check the host in the tab Databases and the address you allowed.

items.q: The data of my cache is gone after a restart.
items.a: A cache is meant to be rebuilt. Keep the data that matters in a place that writes it to the disk, and take a backup of the files from the tab Backups.

title: MongoDB
summary: What a deployment of MongoDB writes into the container today, and where the databases of an instance live.

blocks.text: MongoDB is a document database: it keeps the documents of an application and answers the queries of the application over the network.
This page is published only when the catalog offers the product. The catalog of the platform does not offer MongoDB today, so the page is not in the documentation.
A deployment of MongoDB writes a minimal Node.js application into the container and starts it with npm run start, exactly like every other product.

The MongoDB server itself is not installed by the platform today: {{planned}} a MongoDB server in the container. The name in the catalog is the name of the product, and what runs in the container is the application of the platform until you put your own files there.

The product page of the catalog shows the entry: the category, the minimum of resources and the price. The deploy page carries the state of the entry: an entry that cannot be ordered says so there and the order is blocked.

rows.v: A Node.js application in a container, started with npm run start

sections.title: A database that belongs to your instance

blocks.text: A database that belongs to an instance is created in the tab Databases of the instance page. The platform keeps it on the node of the instance, so it is not a server that runs inside the container.

items.title: Open the tab Databases
items.body: Open the instance and choose the tab Databases.
items.result: The tab Databases shows the databases that belong to the instance.

items.title: Create the database
items.body: Fill in the fields Name of the database, User of the database and Password, and leave the allowed address as it is if the connection comes from the instance itself.
items.result: The database appears in the list of the tab.

items.title: Take the credentials
items.body: Choose Credentials to see the host, the port, the user and the password of the database.
items.result: The dialog says: Copy them now. The password can be asked for again, but every ask is written to the log.

blocks.text: The databases of an instance are its own. They are not shared with the other instances of the account.

sections.title: Connect your code to the database

blocks.text: The platform sets no environment variable that you have to fill in. The tab Startup of the instance shows it in these words: No variables. The container starts without any environment variable.
The connection details of a database are yours to write: you write them in your code, or in the tab Startup of the instance with Add a variable, and you use them there.

The host of a database of an instance is the address that the tab Databases shows. Your application runs in the container, so the host has to be reachable from there: the allowed address of the database decides who may open a connection to it.
The backups are made by you, on demand, from the tab Backups of the instance. The platform copies the files of the container into an archive that you can download and restore.
Nothing makes a backup on a schedule and the platform keeps no history of them.
A backup is a copy of the files of the container. The data of a database that belongs to an instance is not part of it, so you have to make your own copy of the data you cannot lose.

items.q: The container answers, but there is no database in it.
items.a: The deployment writes the application of the platform. The database server of the product is not installed in the container today.

title: Choose the right resources
summary: What the memory, the vCPU and the storage of an instance mean and how the price follows them.

blocks.text: An instance runs in a container with three limits. The container gets exactly what you buy, and the limits are the limits of the service until a change of resources is applied.

rows.v: The memory the container may use. The interface shows it in MB or in GB.
The number of processors the container may use.
The space of the disk of the container. The files you upload take that space.

blocks.text: The minimum and the maximum belong to the product in the catalog. The platform refuses a configuration that is under the minimum of the product or over its maximum.

sections.title: How the price follows the resources

blocks.text: The price of a configuration is calculated by the platform from the resources you choose. The price is in euros and the period is the month.

Every product of the catalog carries a minimum of resources and a price of its own. The page of the product shows the minimum in the panel Minimum resources, and the card of the product in the catalog shows the starting price.
The tab Resources of an instance shows what you bought: the purchased limits, the price of the month and, when a change is being prepared, the price the change would bring.

sections.title: Change the resources of an instance

items.title: Open the tab Resources
items.body: Open the instance and choose the tab Resources. The purchased limits and the price of the month are there.
items.result: The fields of the memory, the vCPU and the storage are filled in with what the service has.

items.title: Write the new values
items.body: Change the three values and choose Save resources.
items.result: The platform shows the price of the change: the new price and the difference.

items.title: Pay for the change
items.body: A change that costs more is an order that has to be paid before it touches the service.
items.result: The service keeps the limits it has until the order is settled.

blocks.text: A change that costs less is settled by the platform itself, and the difference is carried to the next invoice. The service is restarted when a change is applied.
Read [Upgrade or resize an instance](/docs?p=upgrade) for the whole of the change.

sections.title: What a change does not touch

items: The files of the container stay as they are.
The hostnames of the instance stay pointed at the same port.
The databases of the instance stay where they are.

items.q: The minimum of the product is not enough for my application.
items.a: The minimum is the smallest configuration the catalog allows for this product, and the platform refuses a configuration that is under it. Change the product, or put the application on an instance of a product with a smaller minimum.

items.q: The price of my instance did not change with the resources.
items.a: A change that costs more is applied when the order is paid, and a change that costs less is carried to the next invoice. The price of the month follows the limits that the service really has.

items.q: Can I change only the storage?
items.a: The three values are always sent together: a change carries the memory, the vCPU and the storage of the service.

title: Invoices and payment methods
summary: What the billing page shows, when an invoice is written and how a payment is made today.

items: This month (estimate) — the sum of the prices of the services you have today.
Current period ends — the day your current period ends.
Payment method — the method on the account, with the action Manage payment method.
Subscriptions — one subscription per instance, with the period, the state, the amount and the action Cancel at period end.
Invoices — the invoices of the account, with the number, the date, the amount, the state and the link to the invoice.

blocks.text: An invoice is written when a period is paid. It carries a number, the amount, the tax and the state, and the newest is at the top of the list. The state of an invoice is one of Draft, Open, Paid, Void or Uncollectible.
The column Invoice opens the invoice of the provider. An invoice that has no link shows a dash; the amount is on the page in every case.
Before the first payment there is no invoice: the page shows the estimate of the month.

The platform cannot take a payment today: the checkout is refused and the order stays unpaid. The deploy page says it in these words: Checkout is not available. The order was created and stays unpaid. Open a support ticket to finish the payment.

The chain of a payment is in place — the order, the subscription, the invoice, the deployment and the message that tells you that it is done — but the switch of the payments is off on this environment, so the payment itself is finished with the team.
The action Manage payment method opens the billing portal of the provider. It stays disabled while a payment cannot be taken, and the reason is written under the button.

items.q: I do not see an invoice for my instance.
items.a: An invoice is written when a period is paid. Before that, the page shows the estimate of the month in This month (estimate).

items.q: The estimate of the month is not the amount of my invoice.
items.a: The estimate is the sum of the prices of the services you have today. An invoice is the price of one period that was paid.

items.q: I cannot pay my invoice.
items.a: The platform cannot take a payment today. Open a ticket from the menu Support and the team finishes the payment with you.

title: Upgrade or resize an instance
summary: How a change of resources is ordered, what it costs and when it is applied.

sections.title: A change of resources is an order

blocks.text: The resources of an instance are not changed on the spot. A change is an order that has to be paid, and the service keeps the resources it has until the order is settled.

items: An increase is applied when the order is paid.
A decrease is settled by the platform itself, and the difference is carried to the next invoice.
The service is restarted when a change is applied.

blocks.text: The platform never changes the resources of a service that has not been paid for.

items.title: Open the tab Resources
items.body: Open the instance and choose the tab Resources.
items.result: The purchased limits and the price of the month are there.

items.title: Write the new values
items.body: Change the memory, the vCPU or the storage and choose Save resources.
items.result: The platform shows the price of the change: the new price and the difference.

items.title: Pay the difference
items.body: When the change costs more, the platform writes an order for it and asks for the payment. The service is not touched before the payment.
items.result: The order carries a number and is written in the events of the instance.

items.title: Watch the change
items.body: An increase is applied as soon as the order is paid. A decrease is settled by the platform and lowers the amount of the next invoice.
items.result: The tab Resources shows the limits that the service really has.

sections.title: When the change cannot be applied

blocks.text: If the platform cannot apply a change that was paid for, the money goes back to you by itself: the order is marked as refunded and the instance keeps the resources it had. The event is written in the tab Activity of the instance.
A change that was never paid for is simply not applied. There is nothing to refund, because the money was never taken.
See [Refunds and credits](/docs?p=refunds) for the whole of the subject.

items.q: Do I lose my files when I change the resources?
items.a: No. A change of resources touches the limits of the container: the files, the hostnames and the databases of the instance stay as they are.

items.q: Can I change the resources without paying?
items.a: No. A change of resources is an order that has to be paid: an increase is applied when the order is paid, and a decrease is settled by the platform and carried to the next invoice.

items.q: Why does the price of my instance not change right away?
items.a: The recurring amount is lowered for the period that comes. The invoice of the current period is the price of the period that was paid.

title: Cancel an instance
summary: What happens to an instance when you cancel it, how long it is kept and what happens to your data.

items.title: Open the tab Settings
items.body: Open the instance and choose the tab Settings.
items.result: The name of the instance and the section Cancel instance are there.

items.title: Choose Cancel instance
items.body: The button is at the bottom of the panel. A dialog asks you to write the name of the instance to confirm.
items.result: The dialog says that the instance stops at the end of the paid period.

items.title: Confirm
items.body: Write the name of the instance and confirm.
items.result: The page says: Cancellation scheduled for the end of the paid period.

blocks.text: The instance keeps running until the end of the paid period, then it is removed. You can resume it from billing before then.
The subscription of the instance is set to end with the period that was paid. When the period is over, the instance is withdrawn and the subscription is not renewed.

A cancelled instance is kept for a term of retention, thirty days by default. The data of the instance is exported before anything is deleted, and the container itself is removed only when the term is over and the operator has allowed the automatic deletion.
The data of the instance is not gone when the period ends.

The export of the instance is written when the service is cancelled and it stays available after the service is deleted. The billing page lists the cancelled services and says whether the export is available.

The export describes the service and the records of the account: the name of the instance, its product, its limits, its price, its hostnames, its events, its invoices and its payments. It is not a copy of the files of the container — a copy of the files is a [backup](/docs?p=backups).

The panel Subscriptions of the billing page carries the action Cancel at period end for each instance. The dialog says that the instance keeps running until the date of the end of the period, then it is stopped and it is no longer billed.

items.q: Can I undo the cancellation?
items.a: Yes, as long as the period is not over: the subscription carries the action Resume on the billing page.

items.q: Are my files deleted when the period ends?
items.a: The instance is withdrawn when the period is over, and the data of the instance is exported. The container itself is removed when the term of retention is over and the operator has allowed the automatic deletion. Take a backup before you cancel if the files matter to you.

items.q: I want a refund.
items.a: The platform refunds a payment by itself when a service that was paid for could not be provisioned. A refund on request is decided by a person: see [Refunds and credits](/docs?p=refunds).

title: Refunds and credits
summary: When the platform returns a payment by itself, when a person decides, and what the platform does not do.

blocks.text: There are two cases where the money goes back without anybody having to ask for it:

items: A service that was paid for and could not be provisioned. The deployment failed, the order is marked as refunded and the payment provider is asked to return the amount. The event is written in the events of the instance.
A change of resources that was paid for and could not be applied. The change is refunded and the instance keeps the resources it had.

blocks.text: A refund that the provider itself refuses is flagged, and the operator returns the money by hand instead of the platform keeping a payment for a service that does not exist.

sections.title: The refunds that are decided by a person

blocks.text: Outside those two cases a refund is not automatic. A request is looked at by the operator and the decision is taken by a person.

items.title: Open a ticket
items.body: Open the menu Support and write to the team. Describe the service, the order and what you expect.
items.result: The ticket appears in the list of your tickets.

items.title: Wait for the answer
items.body: The team answers in the ticket.
items.result: The answer says what is done with the money.

blocks.text: The platform does not promise a delay. The payment provider states how long it takes to return the amount.
A decrease of the resources is not refunded. The difference is carried to the next invoice of the account.

sections.title: What the platform does not do

items: It does not refund an order that was never paid: the change is simply not applied.
It does not refund a paid order twice: an order whose payment was already returned is never applied again and never refunded again.
It does not promise a refund that it has not implemented.
